utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're the one who will examine the next witness, who I think started his career in this case as a 92 ter witness but is now a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just asked information from Mr. McCloskey about the next witness. Then the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. No protective measures, Mr. McCloskey? An estimate of three hours. I do understand that the Defence requests four hours. Now, usually if it is viva voce testimony, it is one to one. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our estimate was based on 92 ter testimony. But we'll see how it goes with the direct of the Prosecution, and I don't know how many areas and how many documents they will cover now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let's wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I was just seeking to be excused to go tend to other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Keserovic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you give a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. You may be seated. Mr. Keserovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. You'll find Mr. McCloskey to your right and he's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, if we could request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- the caution that the witness is familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Keserovic, I would like to inform you about the existence of Rule 90(E) in this Tribunal. Rule 90(E) states that a witness in this case, that would be you, may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate yourself. We then, however, the Chamber, we can compel -- we may compel you to answer the question, but testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against you for any offence with an exception of the offence of false testimony. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we -- Mr. McCloskey will now start his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you state your full name, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Dragomir Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you retire from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At what rank?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The rank of major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were born in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, near Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's true, is it not, that you were a career military officer in the JNA before the war in Bosnia broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us the -- when you first joined the VRS and where you were first assigned and just go through your different assignments and ranks up until the time that you left service, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I joined the VRS on the 17th of June, 1992. I exercised different duties starting with the chief of security of an armoured brigade, military police battalion commander in the East Bosnia Corps, military police battalion commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, desk clerk -- desk officer and chief of security department and the military police department in the security administration of the security and intelligence sector of the Main Staff of the VRS. Lastly, I was commander of an armoured brigade in the 1st Krajina Corps. It lasted until the end of the war. After the war my duties -- my duty was the chief of counter-intelligence in the security administration, chief of security administration, Chief of Staff of the corps, then again chief of security administration in the Ministry of Defence of the VRS [as interpreted] and assistant minister for security in the VRS [as interpreted]. On the 30th of June, 2004, I was removed by a decision of the high representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Ashdown. This is where I stopped working within the defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your understanding of why Mr. Ashdown removed you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to paraphrase, or rather, present his explanation. He said that as for my functional title of chief of security, I did not invest sufficient effort to have the suspects that were looked after -- that were sought by this Tribunal to be located and arrested --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have one intervention in regard of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 19, lines 13 and 14, twice it's mentioned ministry of VRS. There is no ministry of VRS, it's RS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It could be significant later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd just like to check with the interpreters whether the reference was made to the Ministry of Defence of the RS, being Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'd also said that after your war duties your duty was the -- in the security administration the Chief of Staff of the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. Enumerating my positions, I said that I was Chief of Staff of the corps and then after, again, I was the chief of security administration in the Main Staff or the General Staff. In the meantime it was moved to the Ministry of Defence of the RS and I was head of that administration and assistant defence minister of the RS at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you were chief of security of a corps, can you tell us what corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was never chief of security of a corps. I was Chief of Staff in a corps, that is a command position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you tell us which corps you were Chief of Staff in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was in the 1st Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you first testified at this Tribunal as an expert for the Blagojevic Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was summoned by Defence representing Colonel Blagojevic to appear as a fact witness. However, the way my testimony developed resulted in my being placed in a position where I needed to clarify many things, especially regarding the security service, the military police, and the relationship of command within the security service and the military police. So their mutual relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I seek one clarification, also in view of the correction that was made to the transcript earlier. Do I understand you well that being chief of security administration in the Main Staff or the General Staff that you were holding a military function but at the same time that the structure fell or became part of the Ministry of Defence, which is as I understand a civilian structure, a government structure? Is that well understood or have I missed something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a certain period, the security administration was an organisational unit of the main -- of the General Staff, and it concerns a period of time after the war. Then there was migration. The administration was made part of the Ministry of Defence of the RS. The chief of administration was also assistant defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said "the administration was made part of the Ministry of Defence," does that mean that it was no longer an organisational unit of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was not simultaneously that you held these positions, but this position moved from army structures to civilian government structures at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can -- is it correct that when you say "Main Staff" or "Glavni Stab," that was the war time title and it changed in peacetime to General Staff or "General Stab"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the war when you received a position at the Main Staff. And can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This was in February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe it's break time, Mr. President, so that might be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. McCloskey. We take a break of 20 minutes, and you may follow the usher, Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I noticed I failed to mention that you had been called by the Prosecution in the Tolimir case as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And another question, what is your current position, if any, now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Now I am a professor at the faculty for security of the university in Banja Luka, so I'm a professor of security sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which reminds me, our time is limited here. I think I'll call you "General" instead of professor, so try to be as specific as you can, but you'll always have a chance, I believe the Chamber will allow you to explain answers, but let's try to be brief and targeted. Okay. So we left off when you had been -- you had arrived in February of 1995 to the Main Staff. Can you remind us where were you coming from and what position you'd had just before changing over to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Before I moved to the Main Staff, I was the commander of the military police battalion in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what position did you take at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I took up the post of -- well, actually the order stated desk officer, but I was alone, so some places it said "chief" and in other places it said "desk officer" for the military police in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you briefly describe for us the structure of the security administration in the Main Staff. Who was its head and can you just outline its sections just briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There was a sector at the Main Staff for intelligence and security affairs comprising two administrations, the security administration and the intelligence administration. Security administration had four organisational units, four sections, and they were counter-intelligence, analysis, military police, and counter-intelligence -- the counter-intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were in the military police part of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the head of the sector for intelligence and security in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was General Tolimir's superior, immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And going now to the two administrations within that sector, the chief of security of the security administration, who was that in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that naval captain rank was equivalent to what army rank?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the chief of intelligence administration was who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us very briefly the difference between the intelligence administration and the security administration in the most fundamental way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The most fundamental difference lies in the purpose, the security administration protects the armed forces from intelligence activities by the enemy, whereas the intelligence administration does the opposite, it strives to collect information about the opponent, the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can the security administration, could that also include protecting the forces from the internal threats within the VRS or RS itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: From all threats directed against the Army of Republika Srpska, regardless of whether they were internal or external.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you briefly describe General Tolimir's job? What was his job? Earlier I had made a mistake in your description and you said: Oh, you had a command position as opposed to the chief of security. Can you tell us, first of all, what is the difference between a command position and General Tolimir's position, if any?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir did not have a command function. He had an administrative function, but he was also a part of the command, he was a part of the Main Staff. Other than being the chief of sector, he was also the assistant of the commander of the Main Staff for intelligence and security affairs. And in that sense, he took part in the work of the command or the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was General Tolimir an expert in intelligence, as you've described it, and in security issues?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: According to the structure and other functions from which -- where he served, General Tolimir mostly worked in the security organs, in the security service, those organs. But in this post as chief of sector, he did both, the integrated work of the security sector and the intelligence sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How in particular did he assist General Mladic? For example, was his job to propose anything for General Mladic or did he act independently, on his own?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Just like others, other members of the Main Staff, General Tolimir, in the process of planning and decision-making, provided security assessments and conclusions based on security assessments and proposed to the commander of the Main Staff, proposed to him the manner of engaging the security service and the manner in which the unit of the military police would be engaged, if that was the subject of a decision that needed to be made. His role was to put forward proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what would General Mladic do with those proposals? Would those get, for example, turned into -- careful, we hear you're scratching on the mike. Could those proposals get turned into orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As the decision-making process continues, the commander when he heard all the proposals would make the decision. He would accept or not accept or accept some parts or change the proposals given to him by members of the command, by his assistants. But he would make the final decision based on all the proposals put forward to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if that decision resulted in a particular order in the field of security and intelligence, what would General Tolimir's responsibility be in seeing to it that that order was implemented?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: After the decision is made, then it would be drafted, the person or the body that would draft the decision would be the Main Staff or the operations organ most often. The decision would also have a whole range of attachments going by services and branches, defining the engagement of the services and branches, and these proposals would be drafted by professional organs, including General Tolimir. Specifically, General Tolimir would be responsible for drafting the plan of counter-intelligence support, the plan of counter-intelligence protection of facilities, actions, professional plans that would complement the main decision by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as orders came through from General Mladic relating to those plans, what would General Tolimir's responsibilities be in implementing those orders or seeing to it that they were carried out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Orders, rather, decisions would go through the subordinate commanders who would be responsible for their implementation. General Tolimir or the professional organs would have the role of personnel who would monitor the implementation of those decisions, provide possible clarifications on the matter of the decision, but they could not make any corrective actions or change the actual decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska, the principle of singleness of command and subordination was in force. The responsibility was set and hierarchically established in relation to subordinates. So you would have a higher-ranking commander in relation to lower-ranking commanders. No one else could interfere in that relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And your position in the security and administration as part of the military police, first of all, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The immediate superior was Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was Colonel Beara's immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what was your job basically in February, March, April, May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The tasks of the security department or the police department within the security administration involved professional military police assignments ranging from assessing and monitoring the situation in units of the military police, evaluating the personnel and the manning strength of units of the military police, training senior officers in military police units, drafting training plans for soldiers in units of the military police, proposing the assignment of soldiers who complete training for units of the military police, monitoring the situation of the level of equipment and supplies in units of the military police, and proposing procurement, deployment, and distribution of assets essential for the operation of military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You mention military police units. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence about a military police unit connected to the 65th Protection Regiment located in Nova Kasaba. They've heard a bit about some Drina Corps military police and some about the brigade military police, mostly related to Bratunac and Zvornik. So when you say "military police units," do you include all of that group or just specific ones? How does it work in relation to brigade, corps, Main Staff military police and your job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I am speaking about all military police units in the Army of Republika Srpska, all units, all battalions, all companies, all platoons, and sometimes squads of the military police, all units of the military police in the Army of Republika Srpska. This professional part was part of the duties of the military police department within the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We -- in speaking of the security administration, the security job, you've told us a bit about counter-intelligence and that responsibility and you've spoken now a bit about the military police. Can you tell us what is it about military police and their duties that puts it in the security administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood the question correctly, what I want to say is this: Military police units are not within the security administration. Only the tasks that I referred to are. Units of the military police are under the authority and the other responsibility of commanders in whose units they are, just like any other units. As for the other, the second part of the question, why they would be under the security administration in terms of the duties, there are tasks that military police units carry out which are not purely combat tasks. And these tasks are planned and proposed by the security organs. Primarily this refers to assignments in the support arms, of which there were seven that military police units were responsible for. There were also assignments or tasks that a military police unit would carry out for military Tribunals and military prosecutor's offices which were a certain form of co-operation and also involved the security service. So these were reasons why these professional tasks were placed under the -- in the remit of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned seven areas that military police had responsibility for. Did that include issues related to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There isn't a special service that would deal with prisoners of war, but there are services that do have responsibility for specific activities in relation to prisoners of war. At a certain point in time the military police can be engaged through the security service as security for prisoners of war, or rather, for locations where prisoners of war are placed. Through an escort they can ensure the transfer of prisoners of war from one location to another. There is also the crime fighting service through which they can document possible crimes committed by prisoners of war. So there are responsibilities in certain services regarding the treatment and matters relating to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So what I was -- military police can be involved in treatment of, escorting of, securing of prisoners of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you've spoken before of the professional control or oversight of the security officer, be it from the brigade or the corps or Main Staff. What is the security officer's duty and job in relation to the professional control of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I necessarily used the term "professional." In any case, the security organ has an obligation to follow or monitor the work of military police units. As regards the services we mentioned, it can also decide on the engagement of those services in implementing certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can the security officer do that without the knowledge of their commander, be it corps or brigade or higher, Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: These tasks in the services are conveyed down the duty officer's posts within the military police. However, there is an obligation in terms of receiving a task and implementing it, that service as needed and at the latest includes it in daily reports in order to inform the commander. The commander need not provide approval for military police units to do something, but he needs to be informed that military police members from his unit are being engaged in providing certain services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When military police are engaged in one of their standard activities, for example, traffic control and/or picking up prisoners that have left the line, the standard thing, is that what you're talking about, the commander doesn't always need to order that? Those standard almost everyday tasks, but needs to be informed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about things that aren't so standard? For example, the capture of hundreds and hundreds of prisoners, their escort, their security, would a commander have to be involved in that or could that happen with the military police working without the knowledge or approval of their commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The military police cannot do anything in that regard without the knowledge of its commander. The commander of the military police unit cannot act without the knowledge and approval of the commander in whose unit he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's with that foundation go to a couple of practical documents to see if we can bring it out in a little more real detail. If we could go to 65 ter 5584. This is a document that you've talked about before. And if I could just give you the three-page typed version of it, it might be easier than having to sort out everything on the computer all the time. It's -- and I think the Defence has seen this and -- thank you. And it's not my intention to go through all of this document, but we see if we could -- well, the last page of the document is -- says: "For the commander Colonel Ratko Mladic." If we could see that last page in both languages. And this "za" or "for" the commander, you've told us about that signature before. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We identified it last time as General Tolimir's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As last time I cannot be 100 per cent certain, but if one goes by the basic elements of graphology, of handwriting, it should be General Tolimir's handwriting and signature. I can't say anything 100 per cent, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure any of us can do anything 100 per cent, but you've seen a lot of his signatures, a lot of his initials over the months that you worked there, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this look like the signature you were used to seeing from him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the first page again. Now, I know you've talked about this document, but when you were at the Main Staff in 1995 do you remember ever hearing of this document or seeing it in your work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But are you familiar with the rules associated with security and intelligence and their work, as set out by the rules of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, because I worked in the security service for the JNA too before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the VRS adopt or use the JNA rules?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of the rules were mostly carried over. An explanation was provided that the rules are being taken over and only certain formal parts were changed, and it became the rules of work and service of the security organs in the VRS instead of the JNA. In any case, most of the rules were taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, did that include the entire war-time period, those JNA rules on the security service remained applicable throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just take a brief look at this. We see it's called instructions for the field work of the security and intelligence organs. And it says under that in that first paragraph that it includes intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks, which you have briefly described for us, depending on the situation make up about 80 per cent of the total engagement. And then it says the remaining 20 per cent of their engagement consists of administrative and staff, military police and criminal/legal tasks and duties. You've also spoken of that particular part of security. Does this 80/20 split, is that from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: There was a correction in terms of percentage that was made. In principle, the division is two-thirds to one-third of the time of engagement for security organs. I said then and I say now that I don't know what the reason for the change was, although later in the proceedings here we saw some documents and we could observe that the security organs in that period of time were significantly removed from their basic duties and tasks and that unit commanders used them for different purposes. That could be the reason why the percentage was increased due to the seriousness of the situation the service was in. In the rules of the former JNA, it was divided between the thirds. So it was two-thirds as compared to only one-third.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did General Mladic, in your view, have every right to change that percentage to meet the needs of the army and the country?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the Main Staff did have the right and the possibility to issue instructions in order to determine positions within the system in greater detail; however, before that the percentage was slightly different. As I said, it was two-thirds to one-third. But in any case, instructions to this effect could be issued by the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to paragraph 2 which says the security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form part. Now, for the brigade that would be the brigade commander, the corps the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it says: "But with regard to professional activities, they're controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command." Now, that was my reference to professional control. It may have been a translation issue because I'm not sure you liked my use of the word "professional." But as it's written here, can you explain what that means, that the professional activities are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it comes to professional affairs in terms of security and intelligence and counter-intelligence, we also have operational combination in -- at play in this paragraph. Intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks are usually followed by the application of operational methods. Operational combination is a combined method of work, where several different methods are used within a single period of time to execute a particular task. Basically, it has to do with the methods and means of work which deviate from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry to interrupt. Let me just try to cut to the chase. I'm interested in the professional control of the security organs of the military police. You have described that already somewhat. Could you just briefly reiterate what this professional control that security officers have of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Professional control, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Of the military police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Military police units carry out tasks assigned to them by the commander of the unit that they are a part of. At the same time, as per services of the military police, for the needs of the security service and security organs they also carry out certain tasks. Those tasks are issued to them by security organs and they are in charge of professional supervision in terms of the military police executing them. The military police, as regards any of its services, can receive a task for a certain day or a certain period. For example, it is given a certain period of time to implement a task, and then by way of a report it informs the security organ which issued it. The security organ monitors and assesses the degree of implementation. If needed, it acts in terms of making professional amendments, corrections, to what was or may have been omitted. That is the sense of professional control in the units of the military police, as per services under the remit of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5584 receives number P1577, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1577 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's get one more document related to the Main Staff's dealing with some of these issues just to bring us home. The Court has heard about the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 25957.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document I would like to show you the original of because there's some handwritten parts of it that you've seen before. The document itself is very hard to make out in the Serbian. The original is not exactly easy to make out. And it's not so much the document that I'm -- the details that I'm interested in, but if we could hand that original to the witness. And the Defence may want to see it, just the hand -- they may have seen it before but ... And this is a document you've talked about before, and as I said I don't want to go into a lot of details. Can we go to the last page, it should be page 13 in the English. I think in both languages just so we can see who this is from. We see it's the Main Staff, Republika Srpska, sector for security and intelligence, security administration, 18 March 1995. If we could go to the back page. And we see that this is the chief, Colonel Ljubisa Beara. We also see some initials there, DK. Do you know who those initials are, DK, and LJS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I produced this document for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just tell us very briefly what it is? I mean, we see it's entitled "analysis of the situation in military police units of the VRS." Following and then on the second page -- sorry, that's on the first page. And then it talks about an inspection that was done to create the report. So can you just tell us what this report was designed to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Until February 1995 at the level of the security administration, there was no one in the department for the military police, although it had been made part of the establishment structure, the virtue of the growth in the armed forces when a number of new units were created, new military police units were established as well. They were quite different among themselves in terms of manning strength, adequate commanding staff in terms of the tasks they performed and equipment they had. It was decided to gain a better insight into the functioning of the military police units, and this was done in February and early March 1995. The most important pieces of information were contained in this report or this analysis, and it included a number of proposals. A result of this document was an order that followed it later on which imposed an obligation to improve the situation which obviously was not satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On order by who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: By the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is your involvement and Colonel Beara's involvement in this project a part of the professional responsibility over military police units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This was part of the professional tasks of the security organ in the security administration vis-a-vis the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go now to page 3 in the English, should be page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there are some technical problems with e-court. I therefore suggest that we take the break slightly earlier and have it repaired during the break. We cannot move within the documents. I'm not talking about LiveNote but about e-court. We'll take a break ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and -- yes, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. There still seems to be a few ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still have some problems with the transcript in e-court, but on LiveNote it works. So I suggest that we focus for the time being on our left screen, at least for me it's the left one. I hope that work will be done to resolve the problem also for our e-court connections. I think -- I reconnected again and now it's working. Therefore, Mr. McCloskey, please proceed. Witness, we had some technical problems and it was still not fully resolved, but now it seems to be okay again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General, we're at this -- the document that you drafted for the signature of Colonel Beara about the situation with the military police units, and could you look at the -- it should be the second page of the original in front of you, it's the handwritten part. We can see the handwritten part up on the screen now and it's -- we have the English translation, the first part of it also on the screen. And we see in the handwritten part it says: "Toso ..." and it's underlined. Who is Toso?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Toso is -- that was the nickname used for General Tolimir by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did General Mladic refer to you, what nickname did he give you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a nickname. We didn't have frequent contacts. He would address me in two ways. As most senior officers he would call me "sefe," "boss" or "chief" and Kesir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Kesir is short for your name? Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise the handwriting and especially after looking a bit at the text here we see that whoever's writing this starts out with saying: "It is a disgrace to have a soldier commanding a unit after three years ..." And then as we go through it - I won't read all of it - it says: "Ensure that every MP unit has an educated and trained officer by 1 July 1995." So who is this that's entering these handwritten notes on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Judging by everything that I know, this was written by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page in English. I think it should be okay in the Serbian. We see various numbered instructions: "Ensure that every MP unit has its place and role and carries out its task professionally." And I won't read all of paragraph 3, but we can see that it says: "No one has the right to either stop or delay let alone send to the archives any case. No one is or can be so wealthy to be above the law. Anyone who breaks the law and commits a crime must be held responsible. Commanders do not have the right to prevent security organs and military policemen from doing their duties. On the contrary, they must assist them to the maximum ..." I guess I did read it all. And these are the words of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This is written probably by General Mladic and this transpires on the basis of the rules and regulations that were in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, General, given what's said here, the context of what is said, the handwriting is probably -- is this probably General Mladic or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic emphasises the importance, in essence these are professional tasks that are involved here, also fighting against crime also in the case of military police, the crime fighting force in view of occurrences of criminal acts that were occurring. General Mladic is accentuating the importance of those types of assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is this General Mladic writing these notes or is it just probably General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Again, I cannot be 100 per cent certain, but it's General Mladic. He is writing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we have an inspection of military police units, you draft this long report about improving them, it goes out under Colonel Beara's name. General Mladic reviews it, writes his notes directly to General Tolimir. Is this the system working as it should?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because General Tolimir is the assistant and he's the most responsible person in the Main Staff for security and intelligence affairs and he is responsible or he answers to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And next point, number 4, it says: "Reporting must take hold at all levels." I won't go into that any further, but can you explain to us briefly as you've done before what the reporting system was for the military police units, and why don't you begin with the military police units from the corps.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I think this third word is not based on but it's to take root, "zasnivati," versus "zaziveti," since some units were not in the chain of regular daily reporting and so that is one of the assignments that were given to me, to make sure that this is implemented. Otherwise, military police units had duty service which was also at the corps level. There were battalions of military police at the corps that had squads for military police services, and one of those services was to be on duty, work in shifts. That service would compile all reports, all information about the services in the course of the day, and then overviews were made at a specific time, often that was at 17 or 1800 hours. They would collate all of them and make a daily report that it would send to the duty service of the unit in the superior command, and at the same time a copy of the report would be sent to the security chief of the command that it was a part of and to the unit commander. It went to three addresses: Superior duty service or the military police unit at a higher level that also had its own duty service, then it would go to the chief of the security organ and to the head of the unit, and that is how the pyramid ended. It narrowed at the military police battalion in the protection regiment, which is a military police unit of the Main Staff, where from the entire army, from all the units of the military police, data about their activities would be summarised and then there would be a collective summary report which would now in the same way be sent to the commander of the Main Staff, the chief of the intelligence and security sector, and to the commander of the military police battalion in the protection regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- let's use the Drina Corps and so they assemble their daily activities, their reports, and where do they send their material to, the Drina Corps, and we're talking about July 1995, so a few months after your work.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps throughout the time, their duty operations service in the battalion of the military police of the Drina Corps was to have compiled information about the activities of all the services from their section, from that battalion, as well as information from subordinate units, meaning brigades, make a summary report, and then that report - if we are going by names, by functions - would go to the corps commander at that time, to the chief of the security/intelligence affairs at the time, and to the military police battalion in the protection regiment, to their duty operations service as the service that would finally compile data from all the corps and provide a report to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say the protection regiment, do you mean the military police battalion of the protection regiment or to some place else in the protection regiment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Battalion of the military police in the protection regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in July 1995 that would be the unit at Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The command and the duty operations service were in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the commander of the military police unit of the protection regiment was in July 1995 who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It was Major Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, what did the protection regiment military police unit do with these compiled reports from the corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Based on all reports received from the corps, it made a summary report, it would collate everything, and this summary report would be sent to the Main Staff, to two addresses, a copy to the commander of the Main Staff and a copy to the chief of the security/intelligence sector. One copy would also go to the commander of the battalion of the military police in the protection regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's the MP reporting chain. How about the security units of the corps, what kind of daily reporting, if any, did they do to their commander or up the chain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Reporting is not as strictly ordered in this way on levels between the security organs. It did proceed in the same way from the subordinate up to the superior organ, but there were no daily reports. Up until the level of the corps, the brigades were not duty-bound to send reports every day, but the corps were the first instance that would send daily reports to the security administration or the sector for intelligence and security affairs. Those sections from the corps would send daily reports to the sector for security/intelligence affairs. At the same time in war time the corps commander was the first-level officer, superior officer, who would be and should have been informed about all kinds of information. So a report of this type was also received by the corps commander. In this case these reports, when they were sent to the sectors by the corps, they were not sent -- they didn't each send one to the commander of the Main Staff, but in the sector for intelligence and security with the assistance of officers from the security administration, an analysis would be made of all that information and then the chief of the security/intelligence sector would send excerpts or original -- or directly report to the commander of the Main Staff on matters that he felt the commander should be informed about. The commander of the staff did not get all the original reports that were arriving from the corps, but as needed the chief of sector would inform the commander. Sometimes he would submit a written information and sometimes this information would be conveyed orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "sector for security and intelligence affairs," are you always referring to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "chief of the sector for intelligence and security," you're referring to who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also mention that there is information conveyed orally. What -- would that be urgent information or important information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, this would also apply to urgent information. Then there would be no written report -- I mean, there could be one but also the information could be reported verbally, information that were not final, and they could possibly be augmented or amended in the coming period. The commander would in that case be informed that something was happening and the final outcome would be reported to him when it was complete. So in such cases, too, the way to convey the information would be to do it verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would these communications have the ability to be encoded or encrypted in some way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If it were to be sent in an encoded or encrypted form through radio communications with the option of encryption, then that would constitute a written report; however, at all levels there were manuals, secret command documents, and code books which both superior and subordinate officers had. So by using this code book in conversation you could convey certain information in a protected manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those reports that went from the military police battalion at Nova Kasaba to the Main Staff, were they done via what means? How were they transmitted or transported?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When there was a lack of reliable technical means, then this would be done by messenger. A vehicle would take documents from Nova Kasaba to the Main Staff. Sometimes some documents or information would be sent when somebody was going anyway, but if this was not the case then they would be sent by a special vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document, 65 ter 25957, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- before we -- yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear whether this handwritten page is part of the document, so maybe we should MFI it before I explore it or Mr. McCloskey can explore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can tell you we found it that way as part of the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is there -- is it on the back of the paper or following pages? I haven't seen the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The original is what he has, it may have been mixed up a bit, but as an expert could you put it in the right order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, as you know, we generally try to ERN things in the order we got them. So each of these should have ERN numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit the document into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25957 receives number P1578, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Nevertheless, Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber would like to receive more information as -- now you say it's found together, I don't know when it was found, by whom it was found, whether it's the -- this apparently is a photocopy. Whether it's written on the back of the typed pages or -- we'd like to receive as much information as possible so as to be better able to assess what probative value it should be given in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And perhaps since this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- the General's document might be able to help us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not limiting you in any way to provide that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is -- Mr. Blaszczyk's job to go over the collections in particular documents and because we had so much agreement with the Defence on most of it, but we can provide that for you very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, we know that you're the one that basically drafted this. Did this make its way back to you, General Mladic's comments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This handwritten sheet is not on the second page of this document. Maybe it was on the last page of the document that General Mladic wrote it down, and then when the document was copied it was somehow inserted between page 1 and 2. So this was not part of the document the way we created it. Once General Mladic reviewed it, this sheet was attached which we later received and relied on when drafting our following instruction. So it does belong here but not in the sequence provided in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I can summarise to see if I fully understood. The typed-out document was drafted, was then sent, and you received it back with the handwritten part attached or as a last page attached to it, and those handwritten comments were used to further draft whatever there had to be drafted. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is well understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you said I do not know whether this is part of the document. This is, as matters stand now, it is and is at the same time not part of the document. It was added to the document when it was on its way. Any further observations in this respect which the Chamber would have to consider?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will ask the witness about the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- before but we do not object, but it's anyway too late now since it's admitted into evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course there -- we -- but I said we would have to assess the probative value to be given, a special look in view of the handwriting, so to that extent it's never too late. If something is in evidence that it does necessarily mean that every single element of a document is always fully probative, et cetera. So therefore don't start to become desperate in this matter. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have the front page of this document on just for one last question because I see a stamp on the front page and I see some ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read this stamp at the bottom that's in -- it looks like it's in blue.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it reads command of the 65th Protection Mechanised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you make out the date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The 28th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English we don't have the right page on the screen, which could be the second or the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, it's the third page. I thought it was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know whether this is -- what kind of stamp this is, is this a received stamp, a sent stamp, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: This stamp was affixed when the document was logged into the books of the command of the 65th Protection Regiment, that is to say when they received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see if we go back to the first page of the English there's a little handwritten part up in the right-hand corner, some of which we couldn't make out. I don't know if you can make out any of that up in that handwritten part? We see 76 and then we can't read under the 76. I don't know if you can. And then we see that the original document was sent to the military police battalion. This is a photocopy for the files. Can you make out any of that faint writing that's above that statement I just read?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't, not the upper part. It says at the bottom the report was, and then it seems to have been signed by someone. But I can't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. I want to go to one other brief area before we get into the events of July 1995, something I'd ask you about before, can you tell us historically how did -- as far as you know, how did General Mladic and Colonel Beara get to know each other? What kind of military history did they have prior to the start of the Main Staff in May of 1992? And just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I can share with you what I heard without being able to testify as to the truthfulness. When the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia, Colonel Beara was the chief of security of the Military Naval District headquartered in Split --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us the year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: 1991. They were blockaded in the Lora harbour. At the time General Mladic had a position in the Knin Corps, and he used his units to attempt to exert pressure along that axis in order to lift the blockade around the officers to have them pulled out. Colonel Beara often mentioned it, saying that it was those events and the efforts by General Mladic had the decisive impact on their being freed by the Croatian forces. That is how he came to get out of the blockade for which he was particularly grateful to General Mladic. That is what I know. I don't know whether they had met before that. As for General Tolimir, Colonel Beara was also -- actually, General Tolimir was with Colonel Beara within the security organs of the Military Naval District either in the Sibenik or Zadar garrison. When the blockade was lifted, he arrived in the Drina Corps where he met with General Mladic. It is possible that they had known each other previously, but this is what I know and this is what I could hear. I was not witness to it. It is what we heard in the VRS in terms of their relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From what you saw at the Main Staff during your time, was Colonel Beara loyal to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In order to provide an answer, one would need to analyse that carefully. He was in a way -- and we all were, we all respected the commander. Now, how loyal he was, he was a bit unpredictable. One moment he was satisfied with his status, the next he wouldn't be. Sometimes he displayed his dissatisfaction, at other times he did not. So it is very difficult for me to assess the degree of his loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go to July 1995, to the events that you have spoken of before. And can you tell us when you actually arrived in -- the first time you arrived at the Main Staff in July of 1995 from somewhere else I recall.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived in the afternoon or early evening on the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I arrived from the western part of the theatre. I was with the 1st Infantry Brigade Novi Grad, which at the time was part of, was it the 1st or the 2nd Krajina Corps, I'm not sure given the fact that it was moved from one formation to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were you doing there? Because you've already told us you got moved to the Main Staff in February. We saw the report you did. So ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the seat of my department, the military police department, was in Banja Luka, it was not part of the Main Staff at Crna Rijeka in Han Pijesak, I was assigned together with another two officers to co-operate with some corps officers in going to the area of the brigade in Novi Grad in order to gauge the consequences of losing some positions of that brigade to the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the task I was assigned for the ten days or so in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you came back to the VRS command, was anyone with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Dubovina travelled with me. He was from the morale, legal, and religious affairs sector, as well as another officer from the operations administration. I couldn't locate any trace of him or get information on who he was. We were also accompanied by a driver as the fourth person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the driver's name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I think Novo Ranitovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us where you actually arrived to when we say the headquarters in the Main Staff, where in particular?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: In the usual way I reached the barracks at the command post where the Main Staff organs were deployed. There was a degree of tension. There were very few officers. I learned that in the course of the previous few days there had been an attack on the Main Staff and that it was for that reason that the work of the Main Staff for the most part was moved to an underground facility, to the command post under Veliki Zep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say you went to the command, was that in that wooded area called Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe the Trial Chamber has heard some information about two wooden huts that officers had their office -- that many of the senior officers had offices in.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But they weren't using those huts that day. They'd gone into the underground command nearby; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I object, this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, would you then please rephrase your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've mentioned this underground base. Where was it in relation to these wooden huts where the offices were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It was perhaps 1 to 2 kilometres away along the road. In any case, it is on Veliki Zep, on the slopes of Veliki Zep, but significantly higher, at a higher altitude than the place called Crna Rijeka which is in a valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from this Muslim attack that you mentioned, do you recall any potential threat from NATO air power?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't -- actually, I don't remember any specific threats. What I do know is that over some time there had been announcements and some intelligence information first and foremost that in a certain situation there could be strikes by NATO forces against VRS positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly what time did you get to the -- to this command post area where -- and found out that most of the officers were in the bunker?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the hour, but I know that it was late in the afternoon or early in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us what you did and what occurred in the next few hours.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to point out something I have mentioned frequently when testifying. This is the fifth or sixth time that I testify. I can't recall from memory whether it was that evening or the next evening; however, according to some documents that were shown to me here in different cases, it is possible that it was the same evening, the 16th, around 8.00 p.m. or around that time that I went to the underground command post. I am not sure it was the 16th. As far as I recall when I tried to reconstruct the events and in my first interview with Mr. Ruez back in 2000, I thought at the time I was actually sure that it was on the evening of the 17th. However, cross-referencing a number of documents, I can no longer say that with any certainty, whether it was the 16th or the 17th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you what you said in the Tolimir case, and perhaps this will refresh your recollection. And if we could go to the Tolimir transcript, transcript page 13864 and that is the 10th of May, 2011, 28995. And I'll slowly read this into the record starting down at -- you start talking about documents you referred and documents that the Prosecution showed you. And then you're asked -- page 4 in e-court: "Thank you. You testified before, I believe, that you had a war notebook and that you consulted before testifying in Blagojevic. Were you able to consult that war notebook recently on this issue?" And your answer was: "No. I consulted that notebook and reviewed it before the interview in the year 2000 with Mr. Ruez, and that helped me to establish the timeline on what it was that I did on those days, those ten -- some ten days in July. And since I still had that dilemma, whether it was on the 17th or 18th, after I returned from the Blagojevic testimony, testifying in that case, I went over that notebook again and the chronology of events and the dates that are noted there although there are -- some dates were skipped because there were no developments on those days, so based on that, my stay in Bratunac should have been the 17th, actually." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, undoubtedly I said so, and I did say it was following an analysis of facts contained in the documents shown to me, but that I simply cannot recall precisely whether it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Tell us what happened that evening when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I arrived in the operations room or operations centre that evening. It is a spacious room. At a certain moment I was talking to General Miletic as well as some other officers who were there. General Mladic appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It was around 8.00 p.m., perhaps a bit later up until 9.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When we greeted each other as always, General Mladic told me - as far as I can remember - that I was welcome there; that in the area of the Drina Corps an operation was underway against the 28th Division of the ABiH; that it was organised that co-ordination was in the hands of the Bratunac Brigade commander, Colonel Blagojevic; that it was not developing as fast as it should and that Colonel Blagojevic was supposed to take another assignment; and that it was I who was supposed to take over command of the units involved in order to continue with the implementation of the operation in order to achieve its goal. An order was to be issued to me by General Miletic which was supposed to contain more detail. More or less, that is what General Mladic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What area were you supposed to take command of these units for? The Judges have heard that the Zepa operation was going on at the moment, but you're talking about Blagojevic. So what area in the Drina Corps were you supposed to take command over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The area of operation or the first stage of the operation was in the area to the west of Srebrenica, Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, and Milici, that is to say the Drinjaca valley. That was the area where the operation was unfolding in order to block the 28th Division which set out from Srebrenica to attempt a break through to join with the 2nd Corps in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we are about at the time of the break, but if this is a suitable moment, if not then tell us when it would be approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could tell us what unit you were supposed to be commanding according to what General Mladic told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, there were parts of different units of the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, the communications regiment, the engineering regiment of the 5th Corps, parts of the military police battalion, of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, parts of, or rather, some units of the MUP, parts of the special brigade, and parts of the special and regular police units. Those were the units that needed to be co-ordinated, as far as I could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said an engineering battalion. We got a translation of 5th Corps. Who did the engineering battalion belong to that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The engineering battalion of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned a communications, I think, regiment. What -- who did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The communications regiment was an independent unit of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break now. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, after the break you have another 40 minutes which would leave you with 20 more minutes to go tomorrow. Is that -- you announced three hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, at the pace it's going and the -- I can see we'll be using every bit of that. As you know, these are issues that you've heard other people talk about and I -- hopefully 40 minutes will do it though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I said 40 and then another 20 for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Even better, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course if you could do it in 40 minutes, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would love to try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're not yet through your three hours. We take a break and resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General, you've told us of the units that you were to command. Can you give us -- particularly what was this job, what was it to entail, commanding all these units in this area you've described around Konjevic Polje to do what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: According to the task previously issued by General Mladic, I was supposed to take over command of the operation that was underway. And these units to an extent participated in the blockade of the operation zone. And they also went and swept the zone in certain areas and also in going after the units that were going ahead of them. So both the blockade and the sweeping of the terrain was being carried out, the operation had already started, and I was supposed to continue to do the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does sweeping the terrain mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Sweeping the terrain is not a customary term, a military term. Sweeping the terrain does exist, but when we're talking about combat sweeping the terrain is not a term that is used for any specific action. In this case the term that is being used is "pretres terena," sweeping, searching, combing the terrain in order to find remnants, parts or complete units that were in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to do what with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: When any of those forces are encountered or reached, depending on the development of the situation, combat can be initiated against them or losses can occur on both sides or either side, capture and disarming may also take place. And then it's all regulated by rules of the command staff combat service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or could it be regulated by what General Mladic wanted as opposed to regulations and procedures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot say what General Mladic wanted beyond the scope of what he ordered or what was contained in the assignment. There were no other indications other than to continue with the blockade and continue to sweep the terrain that were given, at least not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, my question was -- and you answered that after prisoners were taken that it's all regulated by rules of command staff and combat service. And I think we're familiar with some of the rules on taking prisoners of war and keeping them and protecting them and all those regulations. If General Mladic wanted to ignore those regulations and do what he -- send the prisoners somewhere else against the regulations, he could have done that, I take it, couldn't he have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
