utterances.text: Well, perhaps General Mladic could say something like that, but no member of the army should have or could have or dared to carry out anything that was in contravention of the rule, especially not anything that would imply the commission of a crime or the actual -- involve the actual commission of a crime, which means that anyone who issues an order that is in contravention of the rules according to the positive rules in force in the army, that order is not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, do you believe that thousands of men from Srebrenica were summarily executed after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say whether I believe it or not. The circumstances and whether this happened in a summary manner is something that I did not see. I cannot really state any position on that. The events and the information that I received subsequently point to the fact that there was unnecessary suffering by members of the 28th Division and perhaps civilians who set off with them to break through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last sentence. You said you received -- the information you "received subsequently point to the fact that there was unnecessary suffering ..." and could you continue from there on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said at the end that I don't know what kind of procedure it was, whether it was a summary execution or something else. That is something that I cannot say anything about because I was not an eye-witness of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you won't say anything more than unnecessary suffering happened to people in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot. It's not that I don't want to, it's that I cannot say anything about the nature of the suffering. This is a completely different analysis and I repeat I'm not an eye-witness. I did not see the circumstances of their capture or the circumstances of their detention or the status that they had in that period or the manner in which they died. So for that reason I cannot say anything about the nature of the suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to that evening. After Mladic gives you this job to sweep the terrain around Konjevic Polje, what happened later on that evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I tried immediately to tell General Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff, that as far as I was concerned this was a militarily unacceptable assignment and that there were many reasons why I should not execute it. It's true that General Mladic, in the way that he usually does, said, "Never mind, Miletic will explain everything." He turned and left the room. Then General Tolimir appeared or maybe he was already there. And then with General Tolimir and General Miletic, I tried to clarify this new situation that I found myself in. And as my superior officer I asked General Tolimir to try to see if he could get a correction or a change of this order from General Mladic which, as I said, as far as I was concerned was militarily unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear about another task that Mladic had given to some other officers at the Main Staff at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I heard about that then, but during this communication in this room at one point I found out or I learned - I'm not sure whether it was from General Mladic - that a group of officers, three of them, was supposed to go to the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade to see what the situation was there and to provide assistance to the commander if needed, or rather, to see what was going on there and to be there as some sort of help. And that this should also be something that would be regulated by that same order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The same order that Mladic had given you to go to the Bratunac AOR?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the document later that the same order contained orders for me and for these other three officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm interested now in what you heard in that room. You're talking about the ops room that night. So what did you hear that night about this other job in the Zvornik AOR?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I already said that in the previous answer; i.e., that three officers would go to the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade to see what the situation was there and possibly provide assistance to the commander and the brigade command in their AOR. I didn't know what sort of a situation it was or what type of an assignment this could be at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which three officers did you learn about that night were going to do this assignment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They were three colonels: Sladojevic, Trkulja and Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From what unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: They were officers from the Main Staff, Sladojevic was in the operations administration, he only just arrived; Trkulja was in the staff as chief of armoured units; and Stankovic was, I think, in the analysis department of the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now what happens? You complained to Mladic, Tolimir gets involved, it's still the evening of that let's call it your first night there. What happens?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic left and then after the conversation General Tolimir followed him out. He told me there that he would try and see what he could do about this. After a certain period of time, perhaps a couple of hours, General Tolimir returned and told me that General Mladic agreed that I should not take over command of those units, but that I should go to the area or where the operation was being carried out the following day, go to Colonel Blagojevic, gather information about what was being done and how it was being done, and report about it when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you weren't going to be commanding these forces, who were you told that the Main Staff was commanding these forces? Clearly you must have had to report to them I would guess; is that right? Who got saddled with this job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: The job was not given to anyone. Again Colonel Blagojevic continued with this assignment. I really don't know if somebody else later took over the assignment, but Blagojevic was the one who began to implement the task and he continued with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear any information about where Beara was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot specifically tell when it was, whether it was the evening or that morning that I heard from General Tolimir that Colonel Beara was somewhere. I don't know if he was at the command or the Drina Corps AOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, we know General [sic] Beara was somewhere. What indication did you get, if any, on his general or specific location from anyone, Tolimir, Mladic, anyone while you were still at the command post either that night or the next morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, no, I don't recall getting any specific information other than that was at the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The translation we got was "at the Drina Corps." Do you mean the Drina -- somewhere in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility or at the Drina Corps headquarters? Can you be a little more clear what you meant? I don't need a specific area if you don't have it, but just tell us what you meant by "at the Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: What I heard, if I remember correctly, was that I heard that he was at the Drina Corps without specifying where that was exactly, whether it was at a particular command post, the second forward command post, at the command post of some brigade. I really cannot be specific about it. I have no recollection of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Will that include somewhere in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Not outside the AOR of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you hear this information from, that he was inside the zone of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: From General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so what do you do the next morning after getting this order from Mladic, as you say it was changed a bit? What do you do the next morning? Where do you wake up, first of all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I spent the night in the huts in Crna Rijeka. Besides the task issued by General Mladic, I received several other tasks from General Tolimir. And I set off that morning towards Bratunac, or rather, towards the operations zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were your other tasks that Tolimir gave you that morning, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: I was supposed to find Colonel Jankovic, convey to him that he was supposed to go to the DutchBat command, and see with Colonel Karremans or Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans about the evacuation of the battalion that would not now proceed via the Sarajevo airport, but would go through Serbia. Also, some assets were supposed to be returned to the DutchBat which the army, units of the Army of Republika Srpska took from UNPROFOR while passing by the check-points, the UNPROFOR check-points. I was supposed to oversee the evacuation of the wounded, the Muslim wounded from the medical centre in Bratunac. These were these additional assignments other than the one to see Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is this Colonel Jankovic that you were supposed to see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic was an officer who was assigned in the intelligence administration. I know that very often because he knew languages he was used as a liaison officer and an interpreter even. I think that he was in the sector for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Intelligence admin sector analysis Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: No. This was the analysis sector of the intelligence administration of the intelligence security department in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, apparently moving away from the previous night. I have a few questions on that. But first a general question, Witness. Could you tell us, has it often happened in your military career that you said that you did not want to execute an order given to you or an assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to discuss myself, but I personally consider myself to have been a good soldier and a good commander. Any order that I did not consider to be realistic or implementable is something that I would not accept readily. There were other cases when I did not refuse to carry out an order, but I tried to have it amended. I never crudely refused to implement and I rather tried to influence my commanders to amend their orders. So I would be part of this group of officers which accepted their assignments and saw them through to the end if in any way possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the -- you were asked to take over the command of the sweeping operation, and you said you found it militarily unacceptable. Could you explain what there was militarily unacceptable in that assignment which I do understand was already ongoing and was continued by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was militarily unacceptable because I was not the commander of any unit which participated in the operation. By the same token, I did not have my command or my staff or my command post or a communications centre. Simply put, I could not unify all of the elements contained in the concept of command and control when it comes to carrying out an operation. The other reason was that I was supposed to go to the area for the first time. I had never been there and I could not carry out any assessments of the terrain or of the units involved because I didn't know what they were, what their capabilities were. So there were many reasons of military nature why I believed it at that point in time to be unacceptable on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now do I understand that you were supposed to go there alone without any staff not knowing who they were and to do a job with your empty hands? Is that really what General Mladic asked you to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, partially it was so. I was told to go to the command post of a battalion, the battalion being the MP battalion of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment in Nova Kasaba and that it was from there that I was to command all the units involved. The capacity and ability of a battalion command post is far below the minimum needs required to execute command over a group of brigades or joint tactical level units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the one who did the job at that time, did he have everything you thought you would need and didn't have? You told us that the operation was already ongoing and you were just supposed to continue to do the same job. So therefore I take it that everything one would need for such an operation was there because you were just invited to continue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Blagojevic was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. He had his brigade, his staff, his command, his command post, his communications centre, so it was a functioning system. He simply had some other units attached. Had I been the commander of any unit, it would not have occurred to me to seek amendments to the order. I would have simply carried it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore what I do understand that the order or the assignment was given to you was, let me say it friendly, totally idiotic. Is that more of less what you're saying, telling us? I mean, you don't get the means, you don't have the troops, you have nothing, and someone asks you to do a job, that is pretty strange, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was nothing else that kept you off from accepting that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no other reasons other than military reasons. The military reasons were problematic from the point of view of implementation. The operation was complex. The activities were complex and that is why preparations were needed, and yet I was supposed to assume command at the same moment, the same morning, without any preparation, without gaining any information, any reconnaissance. It would all have been customary in such situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the second thing you were asked to do was to go to the Bratunac area of responsibility and there you also said, "I'm not going there," isn't it? Three others went. You didn't want to go. That's at least how I understood your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Mr. President. I'm afraid there was a misunderstanding. As for the amended task of going to the area, I implemented it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I mean the one you did not want to implement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To assume command of the units? I didn't carry it out and the order was amended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you said - and I read part of your answer - that you were asked what you heard in that room, that you're talking about the operations room that night, what did you hear that night about this other job in the Zvornik area of responsibility. Yes, you say it was only asked to the other three and you were not bothered by going there as the other three were. Is that is that how I have to understand? That's good that it's clarified --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you were there, the others were sent there, but you had no idea what kind of an assignment that was, what it could be at that time. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't know what was going on in the area of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were never asked to go there with the same assignment as Sladojevic, Trkulja and Stankovic finally had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this moment about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I see it's time to break, but I might just help with a clarification that may help some.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you aren't sent to Zvornik, but you did -- did you get some additional tasks related to the Bratunac area by Tolimir that morning before you left regarding Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have mentioned it already concerning the Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I may not have fully understood, but that's the reason why I'm sometimes asking clarifying questions if it's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day. I have stolen ten minutes from your time today, Mr. McCloskey, which would men that you would have another 30 minutes left for tomorrow. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I hope we can get through then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow or perhaps even the day after tomorrow and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 18th of June, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of June, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
